correctness.rationale: At N=174592 the displayed factorization gives sigma(N)=1023*12*32=392832; the excess over 2N is 43648=N/4. The nine pairs consist of 18 distinct divisors, their products are N and their sum is 349184=2N, so their union is complement-closed. For leastness, 1 cannot satisfy the proper-divisor condition. For every 2<=n<=N the divisor-sum sieve counts each divisor once and near-perfectness is exactly 0<e=sigma(n)-2n<n and n mod e=0. Complement is an involution; any closed subset is precisely a union of whole orbits, counting a square-root singleton once. The reachable-sum update from B=1 is B=(B|(B<<w)) & ((1<<(2*n+1))-1) for each orbit weight w; the 2n bit tests the condition. Positive weights make the truncation exact. A separately written Python reproduction (independent_sieve.py, default limit 174592) returned all 37 listed candidates and sole intersection [174592], independently checking the factorization, excess and witness. The frozen code was inspected, not executed.
residual_risks: The bounded exhaustion proves the least element, not any structural or asymptotic assertion about larger elements.

evidence: Theorem 5 raises an already strongly pseudoperfect base with an included (1,n) pair to positive powers; Theorem 6 restricts the shape 2^k p, p a Mersenne prime. The catalog Findings for 516c480fca5c and 7d2c76c9ad9a treat respectively three and two omissions at omega(n)=3, Omega(n)=4. The indexed 3ed82619b9c4 description is restricted to 2^a p^2, but its full text was unavailable in the mirror.
broader_coverage.reasoning: A power theorem needing a known strongly pseudoperfect base does not generate this witness, whose prime exponents have gcd one. N has eleven prime factors counted with multiplicity, not four, and neither of the two catalog omission counts is the stated joint condition. The prime-square result as described has the wrong support and exponent shape.

evidence: Question 40 asks about a square with its square root as the omitted divisor; Question 41 concerns infinitely many strongly pseudoperfect squares. The result here has an odd exponent of 2 and omitted divisor N/4. It admits a different divisor set of sum 2N, using several complementary pairs.
claim_vs_prior_implication.reasoning: An affirmative Q40 alone would imply Q42 by omitting the unique fixed point of the complement involution, but that prior question is not an established construction of this nonsquare witness. The N/4 omission by itself does not give complementary closure. Neither that possible square construction nor the scope of the Wang–Zelinsky theorems gives the nonsquare witness or its minimum.

evidence: Question 42 asks: ‘Is there any number which is both near-perfect and strongly pseudoperfect?’ Wang–Zelinsky p. 3 imposes sum 2n and the biconditional d in S iff n/d in S, exactly as in the frozen finding.
equivalent_formulations.reasoning: The witness answers precisely this existential question, and the search adds leastness over all positive integers. Ordinary pseudoperfectness does not impose closure under complement.

originality.rationale: The contribution is the conjunction and its least element, not the appearance of N in the near-perfect sequence, or the separate definition or theory of strong pseudoperfectness. The explicit witness answers Question 42. No covering prior intersection statement or sufficient theorem furnishing this example was identified in the compared passages.
residual_risks: An extended private table or differently indexed joint example could predate the finding; the public table comparisons and available full-text passages are not exhaustive.
